sections.heading: What is the Monotonic Stack Pattern?
sections.content: A monotonic stack is a stack whose elements are always kept in sorted order (either increasing or decreasing from bottom to top). Before pushing a new element, you pop every element that would break the order. Each popped element has just found its answer: the new element is its next greater (or next smaller) neighbor. Every element is pushed once and popped once, so the whole scan is O(n).

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Find the next greater or next smaller element for every position
Find the previous greater or previous smaller element
Compute spans or distances to the next warmer day or taller building
Find the largest rectangle in a histogram or in a binary matrix
Trap rain water, or sum the minimum of every subarray
Remove digits or duplicates to form the smallest or largest result
Keywords: next greater, next smaller, nearest, span, warmer, taller, histogram, remove K digits

rows.type: Decreasing stack (big to small, bottom to top)

rows.type: Increasing stack (small to big, bottom to top)

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Think of people standing in a line looking right. A person is blocked by anyone taller than them. A decreasing stack keeps only the people who have not yet found someone taller. When a taller person arrives, everyone shorter on the stack has found their answer and is popped. Whoever remains on the stack still waits for a taller person to appear.

Quick Rules for Choosing the Stack
items: Next greater to the right: scan left to right, pop smaller elements, they get their answer
Next smaller to the right: scan left to right, pop larger elements
Previous greater or smaller: after popping, read the answer from the stack top
Store indices instead of values when you need distances or positions
Use > or >= carefully when equal values exist, since this decides ties
For circular arrays, loop through 2n positions using i % n

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using the wrong comparison direction (greater versus smaller) for the stack type
Storing values when you need indices (distances and widths need positions)
Mishandling equal values: > versus >= changes which duplicate gets the answer
Forgetting the sentinel (extra 0) in the histogram problem, so the stack is never flushed
Calling stack.last() on an empty stack
Computing the width in the histogram incorrectly after popping (use the new top, not the popped index)
Forgetting to loop twice for circular arrays
Using the pattern when a window shrinks from the left; that needs a monotonic queue instead

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: A monotonic stack keeps elements in sorted order by popping those that break the order
Popped elements have just found their next greater or next smaller neighbor
Use a decreasing stack for next greater and an increasing stack for next smaller
Store indices so you can compute distances and widths
Each element is pushed and popped once, giving O(n) overall
Histogram, rain water and subarray minimum problems are all contribution-style uses of this pattern
